Since \(\sqrt{x}\) appears, interpret \(x\to 0\) as \(x\to 0^+\). Let

\[
L=\lim_{x\to 0^+}\frac{2f'(1/x)}{x\sqrt{x}}.
\]

Set \(t=\frac1x\). Then \(t\to\infty\), and

\[
x\sqrt{x}=\frac1t\cdot \frac1{\sqrt t}=t^{-3/2}.
\]

So

\[
L=\lim_{t\to\infty}2t^{3/2}f'(t).
\]

Now rewrite the given limit. Let \(u=x^2+1\). Then \(x=\sqrt{u-1}\), and

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}x f(x^2+1)=2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\lim_{u\to\infty}\sqrt{u-1}\,f(u)=2.
\]

Hence

\[
f(u)\sim \frac{2}{\sqrt{u}}.
\]

Assuming the requested limit exists, write

\[
2t^{3/2}f'(t)-L\to 0.
\]

Then

\[
f'(t)=\frac{L}{2}t^{-3/2}+o(t^{-3/2}).
\]

Since \(f(t)\to 0\),

\[
f(t)=-\int_t^\infty f'(u)\,du
=-L t^{-1/2}+o(t^{-1/2}).
\]

Comparing with \(f(t)\sim 2t^{-1/2}\) gives

\[
-L=2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L=-2.
\]

\[
\boxed{-2}
\]
